paragraphs.text: This leaf comes from Anhua, a mountain county on the Zi river in north central Hunan, widely named as the main home of [Anhua dark tea](anhua-dark:definition) and a starting point of the old tea routes to the northwest. Like every tea made there, it began as [heimaocha](anhua-dark:making), a raw tea of large local leaf, traditionally dried over a pine fire, then steamed soft before pressing.

Bailiang, a hundred liang, is one of the county's [flower rolls](anhua-dark:family), tall columns named by their old weight and sitting between the thousand and the ten. A roll is packed into a woven bamboo basket lined with leaf and [pressed tight by treading and twisting](anhua-dark:rolls) with long bars, then left to dry slowly in sun and night air for weeks. The rolls grew out of the border trade under the [Qing](anhua-dark:history).

Made in 2006, it has now had twenty years. Tea from the area is [kept for years](anhua-dark:ageing) in the belief that it improves, though no agreed count of years marks it as aged; what matters is that it stays clean, dry and aired, away from mould and other smells.

brewing.text: From a brick, cake or basket, ease the leaf off along the edge or from the top with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole pieces give up their flavour steadily; crumbs release it all at once and cloud the cup. In a small pot or gaiwan, use water at the boil and start with a steep of about 15 to 30 seconds, a little longer each round. Pressed and aged Anhua tea is also commonly simmered in a pot.

notice.text: A redder liquor, a sweeter, mellower cup, and sometimes a medicinal or herbal note.
